primary_text_note: Novel in copyright. Quotations checked against LitCharts chapter and quote pages (chapters 7, 19, 22, 23) and the Wikipedia article on the novel.

findings.claim: "For the Eduqas exam, you will face a two-part question on Never Let Me Go: part (a) asks you to analyse a printed extract (20 marks), and part (b) asks you to write about the wider text (20 marks). Both assess AO1 (response to text), AO2 (language, form, structure), and AO4 (context)." The same 20 + 20 split, and AO4 defined as context, recur in the L1 key fact and in the exam tips of lessons 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 7 and 8, and in two L8 flashcards.
findings.truth: The novel sits in the post-1914 prose and drama section of the second literature paper: 40 marks, one source-based response using a printed extract plus the whole novel. The spec publishes no per-question mark split, so 20 + 20 is unsupported. The section assesses AO1, AO2 and AO4, and AO4 is spelling, punctuation and grammar - not context. Context (AO3) is not assessed on this section at all, so every instruction to embed or earn context marks here is wrong. Closed book. About 50 minutes.
findings.evidence: specs/eduqas/english-literature-C720QS.md lines 390-425: 'Written examination: 2 hours and 30 minutes / 60% of qualification'; 'Section A (20%) Post 1914 Prose/Drama (40 marks)'; 'This assessment will also test learner's spelling, punctuation and grammar.'; 'Section A assesses AO1, AO2 and AO4.'; 'Learners are not permitted to take copies of the set texts into the examination.' Compare line 442, where AO3 appears only for Section B.

findings.claim: All 48 practice questions across the eight lessons are labelled "20 marks - Extract Analysis" or "20 marks - Wider Text Response".
findings.truth: There is one question on the novel and it is worth 40 marks. Both labels relabelled "40 marks - Source-Based Response".

findings.claim: All 48 mark schemes run a ladder scaled to 20 marks: Top band (17-20) / Upper-mid band (13-16) / Mid band (9-12) / Lower-mid band (5-8) / Lower band (1-4). Eleven of them also award credit for context, e.g. "Links to AO4 context of dehumanisation", "Embeds relevant context", "Links to real-world bioethics debates (Dolly the Sheep, stem cell research) for AO4".
findings.truth: Rescaled to the real 40-mark total in five equal house bands: Top band (33-40) / Upper-mid band (25-32) / Mid band (17-24) / Lower-mid band (9-16) / Low band (1-8). 'Lower band' was also outside the house ladder vocabulary. The context-credit clauses are replaced, because context is not assessed here and AO4 is technical accuracy.
findings.evidence: specs/eduqas/english-literature-C720QS.md lines 405-425; CHECK_PROMPT.md house band list.

findings.claim: The board is named in lesson prose and in student-facing metadata: "For the Eduqas exam", "The Eduqas Component 2, Section A question", the L1 revision tip "the three Assessment Objectives tested in the Eduqas NLMG question", the L8 conclusion "For the Eduqas exam", and L8 flashcards 12 and 13 ("For the Eduqas extract task", "For the Eduqas wider-text task").
findings.truth: House rule: Eduqas and WJEC lessons must use neutral phrasing and never name the board. "Component 2" is also a banned component code.
findings.evidence: CHECK_PROMPT.md banned-string list; project house rule on Eduqas/WJEC neutral phrasing.

findings.claim: "One of the novel's most important phrases appears early: 'We were told and not told.' Kathy reflects that..." The phrase is attributed to Kathy, in the first person, in L1 (heading, body, conclusion, knowledge check 3, flashcard 9), L2 (body, the partial-knowledge definition in content and glossary) and L8 (key fact, match question, flashcard 1).
findings.truth: The phrase is Miss Lucy's, spoken to the students in Chapter 7 and in the second person: she tells them they have been "told and not told". Kathy is not the speaker, and "We were told and not told" is not the novel's wording. Fixed to the verbatim fragment "told and not told" with Miss Lucy named.
findings.evidence: LitCharts quotes page, Chapter 7 p. 81, speaker Miss Lucy: 'The problem, as I see it, is that you've been told and not told...' (https://www.litcharts.com/lit/never-let-me-go/quotes).

findings.claim: Flashcard answers 4 and 5 are single words: "'Donations.'" and "'Completing.'", against questions beginning "What euphemism...".
findings.truth: A single-word flashcard answer is only allowed when the question begins What is / Who was / When / Name. Both answers expanded to a short phrase.

findings.claim: Ruth's apology is called a "deathbed confession" in L4 (practice question 4), L5 (body, conclusion, knowledge check 3, flashcard 5).
findings.truth: Ruth apologises in the car on the way back from the beached boat in Chapter 19, while she is recovering from a donation. She completes later, during her next donation. It is not a deathbed scene.
findings.evidence: LitCharts Chapter 19: the trip to the boat is Kathy, Tommy and Ruth, and 'Ruth makes her apology in the car during the drive back from the boat'; quotes page, Chapter 19 p. 232, speaker Ruth.

findings.claim: "She admits she deliberately kept them apart because she was jealous of their connection: Ruth confesses she deliberately kept Kathy and Tommy apart, acknowledging that 'it should have been you two' She gives them Madame's address..."
findings.truth: The clause is duplicated, the sentence has no full stop, and 'it should have been you two' could not be matched to Ruth's Chapter 19 speech in any source. The duplicated clause and the unverifiable quotation are removed; the surviving sentence keeps the fact.
findings.evidence: LitCharts quotes page, Chapter 19 p. 232 gives Ruth's apology wording, which does not contain this phrase.

findings.claim: "...his face distorted with fury The posture evokes a crucifixion."
findings.truth: Missing full stop between two sentences.

findings.claim: The river image is given to Kathy at the wire fence in the final scene: "Kathy imagines everything she has lost blown towards her across the fields: 'I keep thinking about this river somewhere, with the water moving really fast. And these two people in the water, trying to hold on to each other ... But the current's too strong.'" Repeated in L7 twice (the boat section calls it "the river image in the novel's final paragraph") and used in the L4 and L7 mark schemes for the closing-passage question.
findings.truth: The river and current image is Tommy's, spoken in the last chapter when he asks Kathy to stop being his carer before his fourth donation. It is not Kathy's and it is not the final scene. The closing image is Kathy at the fence in Norfolk, imagining what she has lost among the rubbish caught on the fence, then checking herself: "The fantasy never got beyond that - I didn't let it."
findings.evidence: LitCharts Chapter 23: Tommy asks Kathy to find him another carer and says they are like 'two people in a river' where 'the current is so strong, it's pushing them apart'; the closing scene is Kathy in Norfolk at the fence with the wind-blown rubbish (https://www.litcharts.com/lit/never-let-me-go/chapter-23).

findings.claim: L4 flashcard 6 "Tommy's scream in the Norfolk field" and L5 flashcard 3 "Tommy's roadside scream in Norfolk".
findings.truth: The scream happens in a field beside the road on the drive home from Madame and Miss Emily's house on the south coast, not in Norfolk. Norfolk is the possible-search, the tape and the final scene.
findings.evidence: LitCharts Chapter 22: the scream follows the visit to Madame and Miss Emily; the brief records that house as being at Littlehampton.

findings.claim: "Later, Madame explains: she saw 'a new world coming rapidly ... and there was this old world, one that we knew was leaving us'."
findings.truth: The second half of this composite quotation is not Madame's wording. She describes the little girl holding on to the old kind world, one that could not remain; there is no 'we knew was leaving us'. Replaced with an unquoted paraphrase, so no invented wording is presented as the text.
findings.evidence: LitCharts Chapter 22 summary: Madame 'describes Kathy's dance as clinging to an "old kind world" that no longer existed' (https://www.litcharts.com/lit/never-let-me-go/chapter-22).

findings.claim: Flashcard 12: "Which Kathy line on the tape captures the novel's emotional core?" Answer: "'Never let me go.'"
findings.truth: The line is the refrain of the Judy Bridgewater song on the tape, not something Kathy says. The lesson's own body text presents it as the song's lyric.

findings.claim: "Near the end of the novel, Kathy and Tommy visit a beached, decaying boat on the Norfolk marshes", and practice question 3 repeats the pair.
findings.truth: Ruth is on that trip too - it is her last outing, and the apology follows it in the car. Leaving her out breaks the link to Chapter 19.
findings.evidence: LitCharts Chapter 19: 'Ruth, Kathy, and Tommy travel together to see the beached boat.'

findings.claim: Flashcard 3: "Which Kathy quote closes Never Let Me Go by equating the clones' lives with the donors'?"
findings.truth: The reflection comes near the end but is not the novel's closing line; the novel ends with Kathy driving away from the fence.

findings.claim: L5 presents a direct quotation for Tommy's scream: "His arms were stretched out on either side of him, his head was tilted back". The same detail appears as the correct option in L5 knowledge check 2, in the L4 knowledge check 3 stem ("his arms stretched out on either side"), in the L5 sacrificial-figure definition and glossary, and in the L5 practice question 2 mark scheme.
findings.truth: The crucifixion reading of Tommy's scream is a common critical interpretation, but this wording could not be found in any source consulted, and the study guides describe the scream as raging, flailing fists and kicking. The outstretched-arms staging is how the 2010 film shows the scene. Two defensible corrections: (a) drop the quotation marks everywhere and keep the crucifixion posture as a reading, which touches six items across two lessons and re-narrates two blocks; or (b) verify against a print copy of Chapter 22 first and only then edit. Recommend (b) then (a). Not edited. ORCHESTRATOR: no source found either way; left as NOTE for a check against the printed chapter 22 (corpus note).
findings.evidence: LitCharts chapter 22 and quotes pages carry no such line; the quotes page's Chapter 22 entry (p. 275) is the conversation after the scream, about Tommy's Hailsham tantrums.

findings.claim: "Kathy has been a carer for almost twelve years when the novel opens" (L1 carer definition, L1 glossary, L1 practice question 5, L4 body).
findings.truth: The novel's opening states over eleven years. 'Almost twelve' is an inference, defensible only because she carries on to the end of the year. Not worth four edits and a narration ripple.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, Never Let Me Go (novel): Kathy is 31 and has been a carer for eleven years.

findings.claim: Tommy's animals are quoted as "tiny, meticulously detailed creatures" in L3, L5 and L7.
findings.truth: This wording could not be matched to the novel in any source consulted. The quoted Chapter 16 line about the animals is Kathy's remark on how much concentration they must take. The phrase reads as a paraphrase in quotation marks. Flagged, not edited, because the real wording was not found.
findings.evidence: LitCharts quotes page, Chapter 16 p. 187, Kathy H. and Tommy.

findings.claim: Two Ishiguro interview quotations: the novel is "about how we all find strategies to avoid thinking about death", and his approach is "the surface calm, and the turmoil underneath". A third, "how we come to terms with the knowledge that our lives are limited", sat in an L8 mark scheme.
findings.truth: None could be sourced. The L8 one is removed as part of the mark-scheme rewrite; the two in L1 are left because they are attributed to interviews, not to the novel, and are not mark-affecting.
findings.evidence: No source found by web fetch.

summary: Every lesson carries the same wrong exam frame: a 20 + 20 two-part question, AO4 defined as context, and 20-mark ladders, when the section is one 40-mark source-based response assessing AO1, AO2 and AO4 (spelling, punctuation and grammar) with context not assessed at all. On top of that: the board is named in six places against the house rule, Miss Lucy's 'told and not told' is given to Kathy across three lessons, Tommy's river speech is given to Kathy at the closing fence in two lessons, and Ruth's Chapter 19 apology is called a deathbed confession. 148 edits; one adjudication on Tommy's crucifixion posture quotation.
